island: Minjerribah / North Stradbroke Island, Quandamooka Country
about: The island calendar. Three arrays: `events` are dated things that draw a crowd, `periods` are the seasons and holiday blocks that change the island's load without being an event, and `rhythms` are the repeating operational patterns that behave like events because the island plans around them. Every record carries what it needs, what it strains, who earns from it, an hourly crowd curve and a weather sensitivity, so the simulation can run a day on this island without a designer inventing one.
honesty: No event in this pack was invented. Every named event had a public source, a record in one of Luke's own repos, or both. Anything that could not be confirmed is marked status `unconfirmed` or was left out.

Every attendance figure is a modelling estimate unless it carries its own `source`. Nobody publishes gate counts for this island. The one measured figure in the pack is the roughly 1,500 people at the final Island Vibe Festival, which is sourced.
Every `needs` number is a modelling estimate. No event management plan, traffic management plan or council permit condition was read for any event here.
Every `crowd_curve` is a modelling estimate. They are shaped from the published start and finish times where those exist, and from the ferry timetable where they do not.
Every `revenue_to` entry is a plausible trade link, not measured turnover. Business ids resolve against `data/businesses.json`.
Dates for 2026 are as published at the time of writing. Island event dates move. Treat `next_known` as a snapshot, not a rule; `date_rule` is the thing the simulation should use.
Cultural events are recorded here as civic load only: dates, places, crowds, ferries, bins. No ceremony, story, language or protocol has been written into this pack. See `docs/CULTURAL-REVIEW.md`.

Added 10 August 2026: until this pass nothing in this pack reached the island. The only door into the simulation was a scan of `next_known`, every one of which is a 2026 date, so eleven records with no published date had never once fired and every dated one would have gone dark on 1 January 2027. Measured on the shipped build, the Friday of the island's biggest surfing weekend showed the lowest visitor count in a seventy-five day run. `src/systems/agents/calendar.js` now resolves every record's own `date_rule` in any year and `src/systems/agents/events.js` publishes what is on, so a record in this file is a crowd on a beach rather than a row in a table.

`sim_defaults.event_visitor_increment` is the one number in this pack that changes the island's population, and it is a modelling assumption rather than a measurement. It is written down as data so that anybody who thinks it is wrong can say so by editing a number rather than by reading code.

Added 10 August 2026, second pass. Three things this pack said and did not do. Every `cancels_if` sentence was printed to a player as a promise and then ignored by the island, because the simulation only understood four of the fourteen sentences and only looked at midnight, when it is rarely raining; `called_off_when` now carries each sentence as testable conditions and the island tests them through the event's own hours. Nothing in this pack was visible out of the window, so `sim_defaults.site_kit` now says what an event puts on the ground and a render layer puts it there. And the island's largest cultural event had an `irregular` date rule, so it resolved once in one year and never again; it is now an annual window with the published dates it has actually fallen on, and no date is projected inside that window.

Corrections made in that pass, recorded rather than quietly fixed: the weekly deal at the bowls club was named after a different real event at the same venue and its hours claimed a basis of published trading hours for an estimate, and the arts trail description asserted two things that are not on the page it cites. Each correction is written into the record's own `notes`.

conventions.status: current = confirmed as running now. unconfirmed = a real event we could not confirm still runs on the current pattern. ended = it ran and it has stopped, kept because the reason it stopped is a civic lever. proposed = Luke's own proposal, never render as real.
conventions.date_rule: kind is one of: fixed (same calendar date each year), nth_weekday (for example third Saturday of October), moveable (tied to Easter or another moving anchor), weekly, fortnightly, monthly, season (a window, not a date), annual_window (it happens every year and the organiser announces the dates, so the pack holds the window the published dates have fallen in and projects no date inside it), irregular (real but no stable pattern found).
conventions.attendance: low, typical and high are people on site at the busiest moment, not tickets sold and not cumulative visitors across a multi-day event. `cumulative` is given separately where a multi-day total makes more sense.
conventions.archetype_mix: fractions of the on-site crowd, summing to about 1.0. Archetype ids resolve against `visitor_archetypes` in this file.
conventions.crowd_curve: 24 values, index 0 is midnight to 1am. Each value is the fraction of that event's own peak crowd on site during that hour. All zeroes outside operating hours. Multi-day events give the curve for a typical single day.
conventions.strains: level 1 to 5. 1 = noticed by the people running it. 3 = noticed by residents who are not attending. 5 = the island's capacity is the binding constraint and something fails.
conventions.weather_sensitivity: 0 to 1 per driver. 1 means the event does not happen in that condition. `cancels_if` is written where a public source or plain physics gives a threshold; otherwise null.
conventions.called_off_when: Added 10 August 2026, and it exists because the panel printed every `cancels_if` sentence to a player as a promise the island then ignored. `cancels_if` is prose for a human; `called_off_when` is the same sentence as a list of conditions a machine can test, and a record may not have one without the other. Each entry names a `driver` (rain in mm/h, rain-today in mm since midnight, wind in knots, swell in metres, heat in degrees, crossing as a state word, fire-ban), a threshold (`over`, `under`, or `state`), and an `effect`: called-off, postponed, shortened (with `reduce_to`), or moved (with `move_to`, a place id). `says` is the short phrase shown to the player. An entry that carries `not_evaluated` instead of a threshold is a condition this build cannot test, and it names why. Every threshold is modelled: nobody publishes the millimetre at which a market packs up.
conventions.place_ids: resolve against `data/places.json`. Where a venue has no place record yet, `place_ids` holds the township and `place_note` says where it actually is.
conventions.confidence: high = a current public source states it directly. medium = a public source states it but for a different year, or two sources disagree on detail. low = inferred, or from a single weak listing.

visitor_archetypes.name: Island resident
visitor_archetypes.description: Lives in one of the three townships. No ferry leg, no accommodation demand, but a car and a strong opinion about parking.

visitor_archetypes.name: Walk-on day tripper
visitor_archetypes.description: Comes over on the water taxi without a car, uses the 880 or 881 bus or a taxi, goes home the same day. Bound by the last return sailing.
visitor_archetypes.spends_at: cafes, takeaway, gelato, bus fare, tours

visitor_archetypes.name: Day tripper with a vehicle
visitor_archetypes.description: Brings a car or 4WD on the barge for the day. The single largest source of parking and beach-access pressure per head.

visitor_archetypes.name: Holiday house or resort guest
visitor_archetypes.description: Multi-night, usually a family, usually with a car. Spreads spend across groceries, the pub and eating out.

visitor_archetypes.name: Camper
visitor_archetypes.description: Campground or beach camping permit. Lower spend per night than a house guest, higher water and waste load per head, and the group most exposed when campgrounds close.
visitor_archetypes.spends_at: groceries, ice, fuel, bottle shop, bakery

visitor_archetypes.name: Registered competitor or performer
visitor_archetypes.description: Entered in the event. Arrives before the public, needs a start area, gear storage, water and a toilet block, and brings supporters.
visitor_archetypes.arrives_by: either ferry, often the day before

visitor_archetypes.name: Quandamooka family and returning kin
visitor_archetypes.description: Quandamooka people living on and off the island, and extended family returning for a gathering. Stay with family more often than in paid beds.

visitor_archetypes.name: Crew, volunteers and officials
visitor_archetypes.description: Stallholders, sound crew, traffic controllers, first aid, council officers, media. Arrive earliest, leave latest, and their vehicles occupy the best parking all day by design.

visitor_archetypes.name: Arrives by private boat
visitor_archetypes.description: Anchors off Amity, Dunwich or Peel and comes ashore. Invisible to every ferry count, which is why ferry numbers underread big fishing weekends.
visitor_archetypes.spends_at: club bar, fuel, ice, seafood retail

visitor_archetypes.name: Backpacker
visitor_archetypes.description: Hostel bed, walk-on, no car, longest stay per dollar spent, most likely to be on the beach at sunrise.
visitor_archetypes.spends_at: hostel, groceries, dive and surf lessons

reference_2026.note: Anchors the moveable and holiday rules for the simulation's default year.

queensland_public_holidays.name: Anzac Day
queensland_public_holidays.note: Falls on a Saturday. Queensland does not add a substitute holiday.

visitors_per_year.basis: A travel guide figure repeated across tourism copy. No Redland City Council, Tourism and Events Queensland or SeaLink figure was found to confirm it. Do not present this to a player as fact.

events.name: Gage Roads Straddie Invitational
events.description: The island's biggest surfing weekend and the reason the brief calls it the Straddie Assault. Twenty invited boardriders clubs surf a teams event and a tag teams event over two days at Point Lookout. Publicly described as the longest-running teams surfing competition in the world, first held in 1983. Free to enter and free to watch, which is exactly why the beach car parks fail before the surf does.

date_rule.note: Runs Friday to Sunday on a mid-October weekend. The organisers call the beach on the day, so which beach is not fixed.

events.place_note: Main Beach is the listed venue. The final call between Main, Cylinder and Home Beach is made on the morning by the organisers based on swell direction.

needs.potable_water: existing beach taps plus a refill point at the contest site
needs.traffic_management: Mooloomba Road and the beach car park entries need marshalling from about 06:00 on both mornings
needs.ferry_capacity: about 500 extra one-way passenger seats and 120 extra vehicle spaces across the Friday and the Sunday
needs.power: generator for the PA and judging tower
needs.beach_access: a marshalled corridor between the contest area and the public swimming flags

strains.note: Twenty clubs means twenty vans and trailers with boards on the roof, parked where the day trippers usually park.
Friday afternoon and Sunday afternoon collide with the ordinary weekend peak.
The beach amenities were not built for a spectator crowd standing in one place for six hours.
Spectators fan out onto the dune face for the view, which is the one place they should not stand.
A big surf contest and a big beach crowd on the same day, with one ambulance station on the island.

revenue_to.note: Saturday night after the teams event.

crowd_curve.note: Two peaks: the morning heats and the afternoon finals, with a lunchtime dip when the tide is wrong.

weather_sensitivity.cancels_if: No rideable surf. The contest runs in rain and postpones for flat or blown-out conditions rather than cancelling.

called_off_when.says: the bank is flat, so heats are held over
blown out, so heats are held over

weather_sensitivity.note: Swell sensitivity is inverted: too little swell is the failure mode, not too much.

events.notes: The brief called this the Straddie Assault. That is the historic name and locals still use it; the current public name carries a sponsor. Sources disagree on the edition number and on whether the 41st running was 2024 or 2026, so no edition number is recorded here. The 1983 first year is from the visit.brisbane listing.

events.name: Quandamooka Festival
events.organiser: Quandamooka Yoolooburrabee Aboriginal Corporation (QYAC), in association with Brisbane Festival
events.description: The island's cultural anchor, run by the Traditional Owners. The 2026 public listing is a two-day gathering at Dunwich with dance, music, food, weaving, arts, markets, workshops and panel discussions. Free, all ages. It is the one event in the calendar where the island's own people are the hosts rather than the hosts' neighbours.

date_rule.note: Annual, and the organiser announces the dates. QYAC's own site describes it as an annual festival. The published gathering dates do not fit any weekday or week-of-month rule: 30 and 31 August 2024, 13 and 14 September 2025, and for 2026 two public listings that disagree. So this pack holds the window the published dates have fallen in rather than projecting a date it does not have. Beyond the year a listing exists for, the calendar shows the window and says the dates have not been announced. Published material from earlier years also describes a longer season running from about 1 June to 31 August with separate named days; that season is carried separately as the `quandamooka-festival-season` period, and the two-day gathering is the load event.

alternate_listings.note: The presenter's own ticketing outlet, listing free general admission for 12 and 13 September and naming Quandamooka Yoolooburrabee Aboriginal Corporation as the presenter. Closest to the organiser of the sources this project can read, so it is the one the simulation runs.

The council tourism listing, and the same dates appear on queensland.com. This pack carried these dates until 10 August 2026. Neither listing can be checked from here and neither is contradicted by the organiser directly, so both are recorded and only one is run. Logged in docs/CULTURAL-REVIEW.md for a human to resolve with QYAC.

typical_hours.note: Saturday 10:00 to 17:30, Sunday 10:00 to 17:00 per the council tourism listing. The ticketing listing gives a 10:00 am start and no finish.

events.place_note: The 2026 listing gives 100 East Coast Road, Dunwich. Luke's own events engine records the venue as the QUAMPI Arts and Culture Centre. These may be the same site. `data/places.json` has no QUAMPI record yet.

needs.potable_water: refill stations across the site; August is dry and the crowd stands in the open
needs.traffic_management: East Coast Road and the Dunwich terminal approaches need controlled flow for the whole of both days
needs.ferry_capacity: the binding constraint. Roughly 2,000 extra one-way passenger seats and 400 extra vehicle spaces across the weekend
needs.power: stage, sound and food stall power
needs.shuttle: terminal to site shuttle, because most of the crowd walks on

strains.note: A free family event three kilometres from the terminal produces a walk-on crowd the timetable cannot absorb in one hour.
Dunwich has a working port's parking, not a festival's.
Everything generated has to leave on a barge.
Late August is already whale season, so the beds are half taken before the festival is announced.

crowd_curve.note: Shaped by the published 10:00 open and by the ferry timetable: the crowd steps up with each arrival rather than flowing in evenly.

events.cultural_handling: This record holds civic load only: dates, place, crowd, ferries, bins, money. Published sources name specific ceremony days within the festival season. Those are not written into this pack and must not be generated. They belong in `data/lore.json` with QYAC's own sourcing, or nowhere. See `docs/CULTURAL-REVIEW.md`.
events.notes: Queensland's Minjerribah Futures program lists growing and promoting the festival as a funded tourism action, which is a real civic lever the simulation can expose. The DETSI page returned HTTP 403 to an automated fetch and its figures were not read. Revised 10 August 2026. Two things changed and both were the pack overstating. The date was carried at high confidence from one council tourism listing; a second public listing, on the presenter's own ticketing outlet, gives a different weekend for the same festival, so the record now carries both, runs the ticketing one, and holds the date at medium confidence. And the date rule was `irregular`, which meant the island's largest event resolved for one weekend in one year and then never again: on the default 19 September 2026 start it had already happened and the calendar filed it under having no date at all. It is now an annual window, taken from three years of published gathering dates (30 and 31 August 2024, 13 and 14 September 2025, and the 2026 listings). The window is shown; no date inside it is projected, because the organiser announces the dates and this pack does not.

events.name: Straddie Salute Triathlon Festival
events.organiser: NXsports, under the Straddie Salute name
events.description: A participant event rather than a spectator event, and the one that spreads furthest across the island. The off-road triathlon is a 750 m swim, a 15 km mountain bike and an 8 km run, with an on-road triathlon, a kids event, an adventure run and an ocean swim alongside it. The swim starts at Home Beach and the hub is Point Lookout Oval.

date_rule.note: The main day is the third Saturday of May and the festival runs the Friday to the Sunday around it. Corrected 10 August 2026: this record used to say the third Friday, which is the same day in 2026 and a week late in 2027. The organiser publishes Friday 15 to Sunday 17 May 2026 and Saturday 15 May 2027, and 15 May 2027 is the third Saturday.

events.place_note: Swim start at Home Beach, hub at Point Lookout Oval, bike and run legs on the sand and the bush tracks. The exact course is not published as a route file and is not recorded here.

attendance.note: Competitors plus supporters. No entrant figure is published.

needs.potable_water: aid stations on the run and bike legs; May is mild but the run is on sand
needs.traffic_management: rolling closures on Mooloomba Road and East Coast Road through the morning, which is the single most disruptive traffic event of the island's year
needs.ferry_capacity: about 600 extra one-way passenger seats and 200 extra vehicle spaces, concentrated on the Friday
needs.medical: on-course first aid and a water safety crew for the ocean swim

strains.note: Residents who are not competing cannot drive their normal route for several hours on a Saturday morning. This is the classic consultation flashpoint.
Bikes travel with cars. Friday afternoon fills.
Mid-May is otherwise the quietest month, so the event effectively creates its own accommodation peak.
A course this long needs more marshals than a small island can raise from its own residents.

crowd_curve.note: A dawn event. Almost everyone is on site by 07:00 and almost everyone is gone by early afternoon.

weather_sensitivity.cancels_if: The ocean swim leg is the fragile part. A big swell or a strong cross-current at Home Beach shortens or cancels the swim before it cancels the event.

called_off_when.says: the swim leg is shortened at Home Beach

weather_sensitivity.note: Nothing here calls the event off, because the record says the swim goes before the event does.

events.notes: Described on its own site as the original off-road event. No founding year and no participant count are published, so neither is claimed. The organiser's contact address and its own copy identify NXsports; a Queensland tourism listing separately describes the event as run not for profit with QYAC and Redland City Council alongside NXsports, and that second claim is not repeated as fact here because it was not found on the organiser's own pages.

events.name: Stradbroke Chamber Music Festival
events.description: Six concerts over three days that turn the Point Lookout Community Hall into a concert room. Small in headcount and large in overnight spend: the audience is older, stays two or three nights, eats out every night and does not bring a tent.

date_rule.note: A mid-July Friday to Sunday. In 2026 it ran 17 to 19 July.

typical_hours.note: Concert sessions across the day and evening rather than continuous operation.

attendance.note: Bounded by the hall, not by demand. No hall capacity figure is published.

needs.traffic_management: none beyond signage; the pressure is evening parking on Mooloomba Road
needs.ferry_capacity: no extra sailings needed; the load fits inside the ordinary July timetable

strains.note: Evening concerts put 100 cars on a residential street in the dark.
Mid-July is winter school holidays and whale season already. This lands on top.
Three hundred people wanting dinner at the same hour in a town with a handful of kitchens.

crowd_curve.note: Discrete concert sessions, not a continuous crowd. The peaks are session start times.

weather_sensitivity.note: Indoors. Weather only reaches it through the ferry: a cancelled crossing strands the musicians, not the audience.

events.notes: Sources disagree on the edition number for 2026 (18th in one listing, 19th year in another), so no edition number is recorded.

events.name: Straddie Arts Trail
events.description: A self-guided trail across the townships: open studios, gallery pop-ups, workshops, demonstrations, live music and market stalls. The published 2026 stop list runs to 33 stops. It is the one event that deliberately spreads its crowd across the whole island instead of concentrating it, which makes it the cheapest large event the island runs.

date_rule.note: A mid-August block. Sources give both 13 to 16 August 2026 (four days) and 14 to 16 August 2026 (three days) for the same event, so both the start day and the duration are unresolved.

events.place_note: 33 stops. The published 2026 stop directory groups them under Amity Point, Dunwich, Point Lookout and Cleveland, so some stops are on the mainland side and are outside this simulation's boundary. The stop list is published each year and is not reproduced here.

attendance.note: Distributed across 33 stops, so no single point ever holds more than a few dozen people.

needs.traffic_management: wayfinding signage rather than control; the load is spread
needs.ferry_capacity: about 400 extra one-way passenger seats and 150 extra vehicle spaces across the three days

strains.note: The trail turns the island's one connecting road into a circuit, so the traffic is between the townships rather than in them.
Domestic driveways and verges at private studios.
33 stops need 33 people who can stand there all day for three days.

crowd_curve.note: A slow, flat, all-day browse. No spike, which is the point of it.

weather_sensitivity.note: Most stops are indoors, so rain moves the crowd rather than removing it.

events.notes: The 33 stops are on the organiser's own page. The dates are not settled: Luke's events engine and one guide give 13 to 16 August 2026 and describe four days, another summary gives 14 to 16 August. The wider range is used so the simulation does not under-book the load. Corrected 10 August 2026: the description previously said the 2026 edition was the fifth and that there was an opening celebration at QUAMPI. Neither claim is on the cited organiser page and neither could be confirmed elsewhere, so both are removed rather than kept with a caveat. The 'more than 70 artists' figure appears in a guide summary and was not confirmed on the organiser's own page, so it is not asserted in this record either.

events.name: Straddie Oyster and Seafood Festival
events.organiser: North Stradbroke Island Rugby League and Allsports Club Inc
events.description: A free one-day festival on the Dunwich waterfront side of the island: local oysters and prawns, live entertainment through the day, market stalls, oyster and prawn eating competitions, mud crab races and a jumping castle. It is a club fundraiser that behaves like a town festival.

date_rule.note: A late-November Saturday. It ran 29 November 2025 and is listed for 21 November 2026, so the weekend moves.

typical_hours.note: The listing gives a 10:00 start. The finish is an estimate.

events.place_note: 2 Ballow Road, Dunwich: the All Sports Club sits in the corner of Ron Stark Oval.

needs.potable_water: refill points; late November is hot and the crowd is eating salt
needs.traffic_management: Ballow Road and the oval approaches; the terminal is walking distance so the pressure is pedestrian as much as vehicular
needs.ferry_capacity: about 800 extra one-way passenger seats on the day, most of them wanting the same two return sailings
needs.cold_chain: the entire premise of the event is keeping seafood cold on a hot day at the end of a barge line

strains.note: A free food festival ten minutes' walk from the terminal. The 15:00 to 17:00 return window is the failure point.
Prawn shells and oyster shells in an open bin in November. The bins have to leave the island the same day or the next.
Alcohol, heat and seafood in one afternoon.

revenue_to.note: Runs a beach transfer to the festival in some years.

crowd_curve.note: Builds on the late-morning sailings, peaks over lunch, empties hard into the afternoon returns.

weather_sensitivity.cancels_if: A November storm cell over Moreton Bay empties an outdoor food festival in twenty minutes and can stop the water taxis.

called_off_when.says: a storm cell over the bay emptied it
the water taxis are off, so the mainland half of the crowd never arrived

events.name: Little Ship Club Game Classic and Reef Rumble
events.description: A three-day offshore tournament based at the Little Ship Club at Dunwich, fishing the summer run of juvenile marlin, sailfish and northern bluefin tuna, with a reef and pelagic section alongside it. The Little Ship Game Fishing Club states it was established in 1975 and is the second oldest game fishing club in south-east Queensland. Most of the crowd arrives by boat, so it is nearly invisible to the ferry counts and very visible at the boat ramp.

date_rule.note: A late-March Friday to Sunday. It ran 27 to 29 March 2026.

typical_hours.note: Boats leave before first light and the weigh-in and presentation run into the evening.

events.place_note: Club base at Dunwich, fishing grounds offshore in Moreton Bay and beyond the bar. The offshore grounds are not in `data/places.json`.

attendance.note: Anglers plus crew plus family at the club. Boat numbers are not published.

needs.traffic_management: boat ramp queueing before dawn, which is a different problem from car parking
needs.ferry_capacity: small; most competitors bring their own hull
needs.fuel: the single biggest island supply draw of the weekend

strains.note: Sixty trailers wanting the ramp inside a ninety-minute pre-dawn window.
Offshore boats take hundreds of litres each from an island that gets its fuel by barge.
A fleet of small boats crossing the South Passage bar in the dark is exactly the scenario VMR exists for.

crowd_curve.note: Two spikes at the ramp, dawn and dusk, and an empty middle because everyone is offshore.

weather_sensitivity.cancels_if: The South Passage bar. A strong easterly or a big swell against an outgoing tide closes the bar and the offshore day does not happen, whatever the forecast says on land.

called_off_when.says: the bar is closed and the boats stayed in
too much wind over the bar for the offshore day

events.name: Anzac Day dawn service and main service, Dunwich
events.description: Two services at the cenotaph on Welsby Street, Dunwich. The dawn march assembles at the butcher shop at 05:10 and the dawn service is at 05:30. The main march assembles at Dunwich State School at 10:15, steps off at 10:45, and the main commemorative service is at 11:00. Almost the entire crowd is island residents, which makes it the one large gathering of the year with no ferry consequence at all.

date_rule.note: 25 April every year, whatever day it falls on. Queensland adds no substitute public holiday when it lands on a weekend.

typical_hours.note: Times published for 2026. The gap between the two services is real: the town goes quiet again between about 07:00 and 10:00.

events.place_note: Cenotaph on Welsby Street, Dunwich. `data/places.json` has no cenotaph record and `data/geography.json` has no Welsby Street. Both are gaps.

attendance.note: Two separate gatherings on one day, not one crowd.

needs.traffic_management: a short road closure on Welsby Street for each march; no accredited traffic control was recorded in the public notice
needs.ferry_capacity: none; this is a resident event

strains.note: Two short closures on the same street on the same morning.
Dawn parking in the dark on a residential street.

revenue_to.note: Modelled as carrying part of the post-service afternoon because it is the licensed waterfront club at Dunwich. No published arrangement was found. An earlier year's listing put a march assembly at the club on Yabby Street; the 2026 notice does not.

crowd_curve.note: Two distinct peaks with a genuinely empty middle. Modelling it as one curve would be wrong.

weather_sensitivity.note: Rain does not cancel Anzac Day. It only thins it.

events.notes: One search result places the dawn assembly at the butcher shop on Stradbroke Place; the article itself says Welsby Street. The article is used. No Point Lookout or Amity Point service was found in the public 2026 notice, which is not the same as saying there is none. A North Stradbroke Island RSL Memorial Club at 23 Mallon Street appears in an Anzac Day listing and is not yet in `data/businesses.json`.

events.name: NAIDOC Week
events.organiser: National NAIDOC Committee, with local activity by local organisations
events.description: The national week. On the island it shows up as school activity, community events and gatherings run by local organisations rather than as one ticketed event. The 2026 theme announced by the National NAIDOC Committee is '50 Years of Deadly'.

date_rule.anchor: first Sunday in July to the following Sunday
date_rule.note: 5 to 12 July 2026.

attendance.note: Spread across a week and across separate local gatherings. There is no single NAIDOC crowd on this island.

needs.traffic_management: none recorded
needs.ferry_capacity: coincides with the winter school holidays, so the ferries are already at holiday load

strains.note: The week sits inside the winter school holidays every year, so its own load lands on top of an already full timetable.

events.cultural_handling: Recorded as a dated week with a civic load. No local NAIDOC program, ceremony or content is written into this pack. Local activity belongs to the organisations that run it.
events.notes: Luke's events engine records a Goompi NAIDOC Community Film Celebration on 31 July 2026, which sits outside the national week. Local NAIDOC activity commonly runs outside the official dates for exactly this reason: the week collides with the school holidays.

events.name: Goompi NAIDOC Community Film Celebration
events.description: A free community evening on the Dunwich State School oval built around film. Recorded once for 2026; whether it is an annual fixture is not established. Council reporting in July 2026 states that Redland City Council awarded Community Celebration Grants funding to MMEIC to hold Goompi NAIDOC community celebrations on Minjerribah, and that MMEIC will hold three events including a community film celebration and dinner. This record is one of those three. The other two are not named here because no public listing for them was found, and nothing about the programme of any of the three is held in this project.

date_rule.note: One recorded date. Do not assume it recurs.

needs.traffic_management: none recorded
needs.ferry_capacity: none; an evening event cannot draw day trippers because the last sailing beats it

crowd_curve.note: An evening event that starts when it gets dark, which in late July on this island is about 17:30.

weather_sensitivity.cancels_if: An outdoor screen in rain or wind. This one genuinely cancels.

called_off_when.says: rain on an outdoor screen
too much wind for an outdoor screen

events.cultural_handling: Civic load only: the date, the place, the crowd, the power for a screen and the car park. events.name: Christmas and the summer holidays
events.description: The long peak: from about mid-December to the Australia Day long weekend. Every business runs at its maximum, every campground is full, and the whole island's infrastructure operates at the top of its range for six weeks straight. periods.name: Queensland school holidays
periods.description: Four blocks a year. The island's visitor load steps up on the first Saturday of each one and steps down on the last Sunday. Camping demand, ferry bookings, grocery deliveries, waste volume and beach 4WD traffic all move together. The state school calendar is the single best predictor of load on this island, better than weather and better than any event.

periods.name: Long weekends
periods.description: Three days is exactly long enough to justify putting a car on the barge and not long enough for the island to recover between waves. The load profile is sharper than a school holiday: a hard Friday afternoon arrival, two full days, a hard Monday afternoon departure.

occurrences_2026.note: Lands inside the summer holidays, so it stacks on an already high base.
The surf patrol season traditionally closes on this weekend.

strains.note: The peak strain of a long weekend is on the Friday afternoon out and the Monday afternoon back, not on the Saturday.
A Monday public holiday and a Monday bin collection is the specific failure.

periods.name: Whale season
periods.description: Humpbacks pass Point Lookout from about June to November: north to the breeding grounds through the winter, south with calves and close inshore through the spring. Point Lookout's headland juts into the migration corridor, which makes it one of the best land-based whale watching sites on the east coast. It is a free attraction that fills paid beds, and it is the only reliable winter driver the island has.

strains.note: Headland Park and the gorge walk car park, mid-morning, all winter.
The North Gorge Walk carries the whole of this load on one boardwalk.

periods.notes: Population figures for the east Australian humpback migration vary widely between tourism sources and are not recorded here. `data/ecology.json` is the authority on the animals; this record is about the human load they generate.

periods.name: Surf life saving patrol season
periods.description: In the club's own words, the patrolling season commences on the first weekend of the September school holidays and continues every weekend and public holiday through until the first weekend in May. The club states it is the only surf life saving club in Australia that actively patrols two beaches, Main and Cylinder, and provides roving patrols of six other beaches on the island. Outside the season, the beaches are unpatrolled and the risk profile of the whole island changes.

occurrences_2026.label: 2026 to 2027 season
occurrences_2026.note: Both ends are derived from the club's published rule and the Queensland school holiday dates, not from a published patrol roster. The actual first and last patrol dates are set by the club.

strains.note: Two patrolled beaches plus roving patrols over six more, every weekend and public holiday for seven and a half months, from one club, mostly unpaid.
Outside the patrol season the same rips are still there and nobody is watching them.

periods.name: The wider Quandamooka Festival season
periods.description: Published material from earlier years describes the Quandamooka Festival as running from about 1 June to 31 August, with named days spread across that window rather than a single weekend. The 2026 public listing is a two-day gathering in late August. Both patterns are recorded so the simulation does not assume the festival is only ever a weekend.

periods.name: The planned burn season
periods.description: Hazard reduction burning on Minjerribah runs across the cooler and drier months and is publicly notified. Reporting on the island programme describes it as led by the Quandamooka Yoolooburrabee Aboriginal Corporation, with Redland City Council, the Queensland Fire Department, Seqwater and Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service running coordinated burning and fire lines across the wider region. Residents in an affected area are notified before a burn, and properties adjoining a burn area get a letterbox drop. What this pack holds is the season, the notification, the smoke and the closures.

occurrences_2026.note: The months are the regional pattern reported for the programme, not a published island burn calendar. Individual burn dates are notified close to the day and are deliberately not modelled as dates.

A smoke day and a beach day are the same day for anybody who has already paid for the ferry.

It is the one period of the year when the busiest island is also the quietest work site, and it is why a repair that could have been done in November is done in February. The simulation has modelled this since the residents slice was built; this record puts it on the calendar where a player can see it.

rhythms.name: Bin day
rhythms.description: Redland City Council collects on the island on Mondays. Bins go kerbside on Sunday afternoon because collection can start very early. For the simulation this matters more than it sounds: a Monday collection means a long weekend generates four days of rubbish before anything is taken away, and Christmas and New Year both fall against the same single weekly cycle.

cycle.note: General waste weekly. Whether recycling alternates weekly or fortnightly on the island was not confirmed.

strains.note: Rises to 5 after a long weekend or over the summer holidays, when the bin is full by Saturday.
Kerbside bins out overnight on an island with brushtail possums, goannas and crows.

rhythms.notes: The Monday collection comes from a holiday letting agency's departure information page, not from a council source. The Redland City Council bin day lookup is an address-by-address tool that could not be queried without an island address. Worth a five-minute check by anyone with a Straddie address.

rhythms.name: The vehicle barge
rhythms.description: The island's supply line and its hardest constraint. SeaLink runs vehicle ferries between Toondah Harbour at Cleveland and Dunwich, roughly hourly, seven days a week including public holidays. The crossing takes about 45 to 50 minutes. Every vehicle, every pallet of groceries, every skip bin and every ambulance transfer moves on this. When the barge stops, the island stops.

cycle.headway_note: Roughly hourly, with extra sailings on Friday and Sunday. Some periods run every 90 to 120 minutes.
cycle.basis: published description, not a transcribed timetable

rhythms.fleet_source: repo:straddie-night-market-lab/docs/research-notes.md, from a SeaLink fleet page read on 11 May 2026. The SeaLink fleet page returns HTTP 403 to an automated fetch, so these numbers were not independently re-verified.

strains.note: Baseline. Rises to 5 on any Friday afternoon in a holiday period and on Easter.
Every arrival releases up to 60 vehicles onto Junner Street at once, which is why Dunwich traffic comes in pulses rather than a flow.

rhythms.sim_hint: Model arrivals as pulses, not as a rate. The whole island's traffic, shop trade and queue behaviour is shaped by the fact that vehicles land in batches an hour apart.
rhythms.notes: Exact sailing times were not transcribed. The SeaLink timetable page returns HTTP 403 to an automated fetch, and the Stradbroke Flyer publishes its timetable as an image. Anyone with a browser can fix this in five minutes and should, because the timetable is load-bearing for the whole simulation.

rhythms.name: The water taxi
rhythms.description: Two operators, SeaLink and the Stradbroke Flyer, running passenger-only catamarans from Cleveland. The crossing takes about 25 minutes. SeaLink lands at the Junner Street pontoon at Dunwich; the Flyer lands at One Mile Jetty. No bookings on the Flyer, and a free courtesy bus on the mainland side. This is how the island's workers, students, day trippers and shoppers move, and the last sailing is the effective closing time of every evening event on the island.

cycle.headway_note: Frequent through the day with extended weekend hours. Exact times not transcribed.
cycle.basis: published description, not a transcribed timetable

strains.note: Baseline. Rises to 5 for a free event within walking distance of a terminal.
Every arrival is a busload wanting the 880 or the 881 at the same moment.

rhythms.sim_hint: The last return sailing is a hard behavioural boundary for the `day-tripper-walkon` archetype. Agents of that type should start walking towards the terminal a fixed margin before it.

rhythms.name: The island bus
rhythms.description: Two Translink routes run by Stradbroke Island Buses, timed to meet the ferries. Route 880 runs Dunwich to Point Lookout, from the Junner Street ferry terminal to Mooloomba Road at the gorge walk, 19 stops. Route 881 runs One Mile to Amity Point, from the Yabby Street ferry terminal to Tosh Street at Sovereign Road, 14 stops. A network update on 1 December 2025 extended the 881 to Dunwich, added a QUAMPI stop and introduced a seasonal timetable with extra capacity for school holidays, public holidays and weekends.

cycle.note: Timed to ferry arrivals rather than to a clock headway. Seasonal timetable variation for school holidays, public holidays and weekends.
cycle.basis: published description, not a transcribed timetable

strains.note: A 400-passenger water taxi arriving at a 62-seat bus is the arithmetic that shapes a walk-on visitor's whole day.

rhythms.source: repo:straddie-night-market-lab/docs/research-notes.md, citing Translink route data and the 1 December 2025 network update

rhythms.name: The school run
rhythms.description: Dunwich State School on Bingle Road is the only school on the island. It takes Prep to Year 6 and draws from all three townships, so the morning run is an island-wide movement, not a suburban one: buses collect from Point Lookout and Amity Point and converge on Dunwich. Secondary students are a separate and harder rhythm. Dunwich State High School closed in 2012 with six students enrolled, and every island secondary student now attends Cleveland District State High School on the mainland, which means an early water taxi out and a mid-afternoon water taxi back, every school day, for the whole of their high school years.

cycle.basis: estimate. The published school bus timetables are images and were not transcribed, and no bell times were read.

strains.note: A short, sharp weekday peak on Bingle Road and the East Coast Road approach, twice a day, forty weeks a year.
The secondary students are on the first useful sailing every weekday morning, which is not negotiable and not weather-dependent for them.
A Point Lookout family with a high schooler loses roughly three hours a day to the crossing. This is a real driver of who can afford to live where on this island.

rhythms.sim_hint: The school run disappears completely during school holidays. That absence is one of the clearest legible signals in the simulation that the calendar has changed.
rhythms.notes: The Anzac Day notice places Dunwich State School on Welsby Street; the school's own material and directory listings give Bingle Road. They may be corners of the same block. Not resolved.

rhythms.name: The tide-driven fishing window
rhythms.description: The island's fishing does not run on a clock, it runs on water movement. The working pattern is the run-in and the run-out around a tide change, weighted by the solunar major and minor windows and cut short by wind and swell. Around the South Passage and the bar off Amity, the tide is not a preference but a safety limit: a strong outgoing tide against an easterly swell makes the bar unworkable regardless of how good the fishing is. Land-based fishing off the gutters at Main Beach and Flinders Beach follows the same logic on a smaller scale.

cycle.note: Two highs and two lows a day, shifting about 50 minutes later each day, on a roughly fortnightly spring and neap cycle.
cycle.basis: general knowledge of semidiurnal tides, plus the field-board pattern in Luke's own Point Lookout Fishing Club prototype

strains.note: Everybody wants the ramp in the same ninety minutes, because the tide told them all the same thing.
The South Passage bar is where an ordinary fishing morning becomes a rescue.

rhythms.sim_hint: Read the tide from `world.read('tide')`. Fishing agents should choose their departure from the tide state and the wind, never from the clock. This is one of the clearest places the simulation can teach a player something true about how this island actually works.
rhythms.source: repo:plfc-community-platform/data/latest-field-data.json (Point Lookout Fishing Club field board prototype, tide, solunar and weather windows), plus general knowledge
rhythms.notes: The specific solunar major and minor window times in the PLFC prototype are explicitly labelled sample data, not measurements, and none of them are copied into this pack. No published tide table for Amity Point or Dunwich was read. The `tide` system in `src/systems/environment/tide.js` is the authority on tide state; this record only says what people do about it.

rhythms.name: Friday afternoon arrivals
rhythms.description: The weekly wave. From about 13:00 on a Friday the vehicle barge fills with weekenders, the water taxi fills with people who have finished work, and by 18:00 the townships have a different population from the one they had at lunchtime. Extra Friday sailings exist because of this. Groceries sell out on Friday evening, the pub is full, and the roads carry the year's highest proportion of drivers who have never driven them before.

cycle.basis: estimate, with the extra Friday sailings confirmed in the published ferry description

load_multiplier.note: Applied to the weekday visitor baseline. Higher inside school holidays and on a long weekend, where it can double again.

strains.note: Unfamiliar drivers, dusk, and wildlife on the road at exactly the same hour. This is the island's highest-risk driving window of the week.
Both FoodWorks stores restock by barge. A Friday run on the shelves is not replaced until the next delivery.

rhythms.source: https://stradbrokeisland.com/getting-here/by-ferry/, plus general knowledge of the pattern

rhythms.name: Sunday afternoon departures
rhythms.description: The mirror of Friday, and worse, because it is compressed. Checkout is late morning, the beach is good until mid-afternoon, and then everybody wants the same three sailings. The barge queue at Dunwich forms on Junner Street. The islanders' own rule is to either leave early or stay for dinner, and the businesses that do well on a Sunday are the ones that give people a reason to take the later boat.

cycle.basis: estimate, with the extra Sunday sailings confirmed in the published ferry description

load_multiplier.note: Departure load, not arrival load. The island empties rather than fills.

strains.note: The single most reliable queue on the island's calendar. It happens every week and it surprises people every week.
Queue spillback onto Junner Street blocks the town for everyone who is not leaving.
Holiday houses and campgrounds all empty their bins on the same afternoon, against a Monday collection.

revenue_to.note: Directly benefits from people choosing the later boat.
Sunday barefoot bowls competes with the departure window for the same people.

rhythms.sim_hint: This is the best small civic puzzle in the pack. Anything that gives departing visitors a reason to take a later sailing flattens the queue without adding a single sailing.
rhythms.source: https://stradbrokeisland.com/getting-here/by-ferry/, plus general knowledge of the pattern

rhythms.name: The waste transfer station rhythm
rhythms.description: Everything the island throws away is handled at the North Stradbroke Island Recycling and Waste Centre at Dunwich and then leaves by barge. That is the whole story of waste on this island: there is no landfill capacity to grow into, only barge slots. Peak weekends and holiday periods generate volume faster than the barge schedule removes it, and the shortfall sits on the island until it can go.

cycle.note: Public opening hours are published for the facility; the barge removal schedule for waste is not public and is not recorded here.

strains.note: Rises to 5 in the summer holidays and after any large event.
Waste going out competes for barge deck space with visitors coming in, on the same sailings.

rhythms.sim_hint: Model waste as a stock with an outflow limited by barge slots, not as a rate that clears itself. That single choice makes every event in this pack cost something real.
rhythms.notes: No public data on the waste removal schedule, tonnage, barge slot allocation or the facility's capacity was found. This is the largest unfilled gap in the pack for anyone modelling event load honestly.

rhythms.name: The council meeting
rhythms.description: The decisions this island lives with are taken in a chamber on the mainland. Redland City Council holds its general meeting monthly, on a Wednesday, from 9.30am, in the council chambers on Bloomfield Street at Cleveland. For an islander who wants to be in the room rather than watching the webcast, that is a 6.30am water taxi, a bus, a morning in a public gallery and an afternoon boat home: a whole working day for one agenda item. That asymmetry is the single most island-specific fact about how this place is governed, and it is why the civic board in this build cares so much about who decides.

cycle.venue: Council chambers, Administration Building, Bloomfield Street, Cleveland
cycle.basis: The weekday, the time and the venue are published. Two 2026 general meetings were observed on Wednesday 15 April and Wednesday 20 May, which is a third Wednesday and then a third Wednesday, but the council publishes a schedule rather than a rule and the rule was not read.

strains.note: A day of leave to speak for three minutes. This is the reason island deputations are rarer than mainland ones and it is not apathy.

rhythms.sim_hint: A consultation that closes the day after a general meeting, and a general meeting that lands on a day the crossing is cancelled, are two civic failures this island can actually have. src/systems/civic/consultation.js owns the first and src/systems/movement/ferry.js already produces the second.
rhythms.notes: The council publishes agendas, minutes and a webcast. Nothing about the content of any meeting is held in this pack.

rhythms.name: The peak timetable and the holiday fare
rhythms.description: The crossing is not one service all year. On public holidays and through the summer peak the operator publishes a surcharge and runs a peak timetable, so the same trip costs more and the same day has more sailings on it. Published for the 2025 to 2026 summer: a A$20 surcharge on public holidays and across the peak from 22 December to 4 January, and again on 26 January. Every event in this pack that lands on a public holiday inherits this.

cycle.basis: The surcharge and the 2025 to 2026 peak dates are published. That the same pattern repeats each year is inferred and is not published.

strains.note: A peak timetable is more sailings on a deck that is already the island's hard ceiling. data/transport.json holds the vessel capacities.
A resident crossing on a public holiday pays the visitor's surcharge for the same water.

rhythms.sim_hint: The vehicle deck and the walk-on seats in src/systems/movement/ferry.js are built from the timetable variants in data/transport.json. A peak day should select the peak variant and a public holiday should carry the fare, and the calendar already knows which days those are.
rhythms.notes: No 2026 to 2027 peak window is published yet. The dates above are last summer's and are labelled as such rather than rolled forward.

sim_defaults.attendance_noise: Apply a deterministic jitter from `world.rng.stream('events')`, plus or minus 20 per cent on `typical`, clamped to the low and high bounds. Never `Math.random`.
sim_defaults.weather_coupling: Multiply attendance by (1 - sensitivity * severity) for each active driver, then apply `cancels_if` as a hard gate.
sim_defaults.load_multiplier_application: Period multipliers multiply the visitor baseline only. They never multiply the resident population.

event_visitor_increment.about: How much of an event's on-site crowd would not otherwise have been on the island that day. It is the only number in this pack that the visitor model may add, because everything else about an event is people who were already here standing somewhere different. A day tripper at the markets on a school-holiday Sunday was probably coming anyway; a boardrider from Lennox Head at the October teams event was not.
event_visitor_increment.applied_to: attendance.typical, after the weather coupling and the deterministic jitter above
event_visitor_increment.how: Sum archetype_mix[a] * by_archetype[a] across the record's mix, unless by_category names the record's category, in which case that value wins outright.
event_visitor_increment.by_category_note: Christmas, Easter and New Year are already the school holiday and long weekend load multipliers that the visitor model has applied since it was written. Counting them again as events would put several thousand people on the island who are already counted.
event_visitor_increment.stays_overnight_note: These sleep on the island, so on the second and third day of a multi-day event they are already here and are not counted again. Everybody else is a fresh crossing every day. Getting this wrong triples the boat load of every festival in the pack, which is what the first attempt at this did.
event_visitor_increment.keeping_the_year_honest: The annual visitor total in data/residents.json is a measured figure that already includes everybody who came for a festival. So the modelled event draw is carved out of that total rather than added on top of it: src/systems/agents/visitors.js sums a year of this increment at boot and takes it off the baseline before calibrating. Adding it on top would make the island's year bigger than the only measured number anybody has published about it.
event_visitor_increment.basis: A modelling assumption. Nobody publishes where an event crowd came from. It is written here rather than in code so it can be argued with, and every figure in it is a judgement rather than a measurement.

sim_defaults.strain_to_consequence: A strain at level 5 should produce a visible failure in the world: a queue that does not clear before the last sailing, a bin that overflows, a car park that turns cars away, a patrol that cannot be filled. If nothing fails at level 5, the number is decoration.

site_kit.about: What an event puts on the ground. Added 10 August 2026, because until then nothing in this pack was visible out of the window: an island holding fourteen hundred people at a festival looked exactly like the same island on a Tuesday. `src/render/layers/eventsite.js` reads this table and nothing else decides what appears. It lives here rather than in the layer so that anybody who thinks a market does not look like this can say so by editing a number.
site_kit.what_is_drawn: Ordinary hire gear: white pop-up marquees, a stage deck, portable toilets, wheelie bins, plain feather banners and a bunting line. Nothing is branded, nothing carries a design, no signage carries readable text, and nothing cultural is drawn anywhere. A record carrying `cultural_handling` gets the same plain marquees and bins as a footy carnival, because the dates, the crowd, the bins and the ferries are the whole of what this project holds about it. See `data/lore.json` prohibitions.
site_kit.scaling: marquees = round(sqrt(people expected on site at the peak) * marquee_per_sqrt), clamped to min and max. The expected figure is the day's, after the deterministic jitter and after the weather, so a wet market has fewer stalls up than a fine one and a called-off event has none. Toilets and bins are the record's own `needs.toilets_extra` and `needs.waste_extra_bins`, not a number from this table.
site_kit.timing: The kit goes up over `raise_minutes` before the record's own crowd curve first rises above `curve_open`, and comes down over `pack_down_minutes` after it drops back. So a market on a Sunday morning is marquees going up in the half-light and a paddock again by two.
site_kit.basis: Every number here is a modelling estimate. No event's site plan, marquee count or bump-in time is published for any event on this island.

market.note: A row of pop-ups on the grass beside the greens, which is what the fortnightly market is.

cultural.note: Plain hire gear only. Nothing about the programme is held in this project and nothing about it is drawn.

music-arts.note: Chamber music is indoors in a hall that is already built and already drawn.

arts.note: The trail is signage, not a showground. Its crowd is spread over thirty-three stops, so what you see from the air is banners at the townships rather than a marquee field.

surfing.note: Contest tents above the high water mark and banners on the sand. No judging tower is drawn, because none is modelled.

fishing-competition.note: The boats are the event and they are out. What is on the ground is the weigh-in.

junior-sport.note: Nippers is a club tent and beach flags, and the flags move to whichever beach the club picked that morning.

volunteer-environment.note: A sign-on table under one marquee and a stack of bags, which is what a clean-up looks like from anywhere.

commemoration.note: Anzac Day puts nothing on the ground but people. No marquee is drawn for it and that is the correct picture.

club-night.note: It happens inside a club that is already built and already drawn. A board out the front is the whole of it.

seasonal-peak.note: Christmas, Easter and New Year are load periods rather than staged events. Nothing goes on the ground for them, because nobody puts anything on the ground for them.
